::: {#rem-prediction-vs-confidence-interval}
#### Prediction intervals versus confidence intervals

A [confidence interval](inference.qmd#def-confidence-interval)
covers a fixed parameter, such as the mean $\mean$.
A prediction interval (@def-prediction-interval)
covers a random quantity,
such as a new outcome,
or, in the example above, the mean $\bar X^*$ of $m$ new observations.
Its probability accounts for the randomness of the new observations,
not only of the observed data.

In the Gaussian example above,
the standard error of $\hmean = \bar X$ is $\sdpar / \sqrt{n}$,
so the two intervals,
the [Wald confidence interval](#def-wald-ci) for $\mean$
and the prediction interval for $\bar X^*$, are

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\hmean \pm z_{1 - \siglevel/2} \, \sdpar \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}}
&& \text{(confidence interval for $\mean$)}\\
&\hmean \pm z_{1 - \siglevel/2} \, \sdpar \sqrt{\frac{1}{m} + \frac{1}{n}}
&& \text{(prediction interval for $\bar X^*$)}
\end{aligned}
$$

The prediction interval is always the wider of the two,
because its variance has the extra term $\varpar / m$,
the variance of the new observations' mean.
As $n$ grows,
the width of the confidence interval shrinks to 0,
but the width of the prediction interval shrinks only to $2 z_{1 - \siglevel/2} \, \sdpar / \sqrt{m}$:
more data pins down $\mean$,
but cannot remove the randomness of the new observations.
The same contrast holds in regression,
between a confidence interval for the conditional mean $\E{Y \mid X = x}$
and a prediction interval for a new outcome $Y$ at $X = x$.
:::
